job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Tara Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now, in your job hunt, your first job or your studies.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work as a junior software tester at a company in Coventry that makes route-planning software for delivery firms. I started five months ago on a graduate contract. Most of my day is running test scripts, logging bugs, and telling the developers when their latest change broke something. I studied computer science at a mid-ranking university, passed with an average mark and never got an internship, so this job felt like winning a prize. I share a flat with my friend Priya and we split every bill down to the penny. My parents run a small bakery and they can't help with money, so the student loan is all mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected and I'm fine with it. At work I'd tell my team lead Dalia that the auto-suggest tools help with writing test cases a bit, which is true, I use one now and then. To friends I'd say good, let's all have a quieter life. Online I'd probably say that tech companies should be honest when a tool is just fancy autocomplete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my situation stays tight but steady. I get paid just enough, I owe a big loan, and I've got maybe three weeks of expenses saved. If nothing changes, then I just need to stay useful and not get laid off when the company has a bad quarter. We lost a client in the summer and everyone got nervous, and that's what I think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and try to be the tester who also writes the automated tests, because that's the way to be harder to drop. I'd put £60 a month into savings. I'd keep using the AI helper for the boring parts, but I'd check everything it writes. And I'd get Priya to come with me to a local tech meetup, because networking terrifies me alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine, honestly. A bit boring, which is a luxury. I'd still be a little tense about the money, but not about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned losing a client in the summer. What happened, and how did it feel at your desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our biggest customer, a parcel firm, moved to a cheaper supplier. Two contractors weren't renewed the next week, and nobody said a word to us juniors about our own contracts. I sat there testing a feature for a client who'd already left. That's the kind of worry I carry that has nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your own contract isn't renewed, what's your plan B?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to every testing and support job within an hour of Coventry, and there aren't that many. I'd also ask my old lecturer Dr Hale for a reference. My real plan B is living on very little, because my loan repayment stays the same no matter what. I haven't told my parents how thin it is.

say: I'd say it's what I expected, and tech firms should be **honest** about fancy autocomplete.
I'd tell my team lead Dalia the AI helper saves a **little** time.
think: Privately my money stays **tight** but steady, with about three weeks saved.
Losing a client last summer made me fear a **layoff**, whatever AI does.
do: Learn to write **automated** tests so I'm harder to drop.
Go to a local tech **meetup** with my flatmate Priya.
feel: Fine and a bit **boring**, which feels like a luxury.
S0.quote: I sat there testing a feature for a client who'd already left. That's the kind of worry I carry that has nothing to do with AI.
fieldNote: Her worry is firm **stability**, not AI; she names the lost client without being asked.
Plan B is thin because the loan repayment doesn't flex.
She is protecting her parents from the real numbers.

steps.text: Learn to write automated tests alongside the manual ones
Put £60 a month into a savings account
Keep testing the route software and ask Dalia about renewal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already happening in our team. Dalia told us last week that the tool can draft test cases from a feature description, and she wants us to review them rather than write them. At lunch I'd say it's good for speed and bad for people who test for a living. Online I'd say governments need to put money into retraining and make firms report how many entry jobs they cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is mostly the stuff that gets automated first. Running scripts and logging bugs is the part a machine does for free. What's left is judgement, like noticing a feature feels wrong even when it passes. I'm not sure I'm good enough at that yet, and the firm is already hiring fewer juniors. The graduate before me wasn't replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get serious about the AI tools, properly, not now and then. I'd also take a cloud certificate course online, about £200, because it's something I can show. I'd cut my takeaways and my gym membership. And I'd talk to Priya about whether we move somewhere cheaper, since our rent is going up in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like running up a down escalator. I'm not panicking, but I'm very aware that I have to move faster just to stay in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said what's left is judgement. Give me an example from your own work.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a delivery-time screen showed the right numbers but the font made the late deliveries look the same colour as the on-time ones. All the scripts passed. I noticed it because I tried it like a driver in a hurry would. A machine could probably learn that too, but nobody's built it into our tool yet, so I want to be the one who does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya about moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm not worried about us, I'm worried about the rent figure. We'd look at a smaller place in Earlsdon or further out, even if that means a longer bus ride. We're not wasteful, so we'd cut the extras first. Priya's job is in a school office and she thinks she's safe, which makes me a bit jealous.

say: I'd say AI suits **speed** but hurts people who test for a living.
I'd call for **retraining** money and firms reporting entry-level jobs they cut.
think: Running scripts and logging bugs is the part a machine does **free**.
The graduate before me wasn't **replaced**, so I'm unsure I'm good enough at judgement.
do: Use AI tools **properly** every day, not now and then.
Take a **cloud** certificate course online for about £200.
Cut takeaways and gym, and look at a **cheaper** flat.
feel: Like running up a **down escalator**, moving faster just to stay in place.
S1.quote: I'm not panicking, but I'm very aware that I have to move faster just to stay in place.
fieldNote: She used her own work for a clear **example** of human judgement, which gives her plan credibility.
Her steady style shows in a modest, specific plan and a cost she can name.
A small envy of her flatmate's safer job slipped out.

steps.text: Use the AI helper every day to draft and review test cases
Finish a £200 online cloud certificate by spring
Cancel the gym and stop takeaways
Look at a cheaper flat with Priya before the rent rises

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is crazy and that the people in charge are acting like it isn't. At work I'd keep it small and ask Dalia directly what the firm's plan is. To friends I'd say start putting money aside and learn a trade skill. Online I'd back a public jobs guarantee and a tax on firms that replace workers with software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone in the first year or two. A tester is exactly what a thinking AI replaces, and I'd have only a year or so of income before they cut juniors. I have a loan that doesn't care. I think about my parents' bakery too, because if I'm out of work I can't even go back there and help in the shop, since they can barely pay themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything to rent, food and the loan within a week. I'd start an electrician or heating-engineer course at the local college, because the robots reach hands-on work around 2031. I'd also ask my parents if I could sleep above the bakery for a few months, even though I'd hate asking. And I'd go to every union and community meeting about support I could find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing at the edge of something. I'd be scared, but I'd also be angry that nobody planned for this when they sold us all this degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate asking your parents. What's holding you back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride, mostly. They worked fourteen-hour days so I could go to university, and coming home with nothing would feel like I wasted that. But if the choice is the bakery loft or missing loan payments, I'd take the loft. I'd help in the shop at five in the morning to pay my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd back a tax on firms. Would you say that at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at my firm, no. Dalia is fair, but the owner wouldn't enjoy hearing it from a junior. I'd say it online under my first name only. That's the gap you mean, isn't it, between what I'd say and what I think? It's wide.

say: I'd say two years is **crazy** and ask Dalia what the firm's plan is.
I'd back a public **jobs guarantee** and a tax on firms that swap workers for software.
think: Privately I expect my job to be **gone** within two years.
I can't even go back to my parents' **bakery** because they can barely pay themselves.
do: Cut everything to **rent**, food and the loan within a week.
Start a **heating-engineer** course at the local college.
Ask my parents if I can sleep above the **bakery**.
feel: Standing at an **edge**, scared, and angry nobody planned for this.
S2.quote: If the choice is the bakery loft or missing loan payments, I'd take the loft. I'd help in the shop at five in the morning to pay my way.
fieldNote: She names the **gap** between public and private herself, which shows self-awareness.
Pride is the obstacle to asking family for help, not lack of options.
The hands-on retraining plan rests on the 3-year robot lag.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and the loan within a week
Start a heating-engineer course at the local college
Ask my parents to let me sleep above the bakery
Attend meetings backing a public jobs guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real warning and we should use it. At work I'd bring it up in a team meeting and ask whether the firm will train testers into something else. To friends I'd say pick a direction now. Online I'd push for training that pays a wage, because people can't afford to study for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's scary but it's workable. In five years I could clear a good chunk of the loan if I stay in work and live cheaply. I'd like to be in a role that checks and directs AI rather than competing with it. I'm not the fastest learner, but once something is proven to work, I get on board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time online degree module in data or software quality, about one evening a week. I'd save £100 a month towards a six-week cushion. I'd use the AI tools daily so I know their weaknesses. And I'd start looking, a year in, at jobs in cyber-security or in safety checks, where a person still signs off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay. Not carefree, but I can see a path with steps. That's much better than being told to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a part-time degree module rather than a short course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A short course gives me a certificate, but a module counts towards something. The loan already covers a lot, so I'd pick one that's cheap per module and that my firm might part-fund. I'd ask Dalia about that in the first month. If they say no, I'd still do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the five years pass and nothing much has changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've got a better qualification and a bit more savings, and I'm not wasting anything. I'd be annoyed about the evenings but not sorry. The only real loss would be if I'd quit the job early for something that never came.

I'd push for training that pays a **wage**.
think: Five years could clear a good chunk of the **loan** if I stay in work.

Save **£100** a month towards a six-week cushion.
Use AI tools **daily** to learn their weaknesses.
feel: Okay, not carefree, but I can see a **path** with steps.
S3.quote: A short course gives me a certificate, but a module counts towards something.
fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a **sequence** of steps, typical of her steady, proven-first style.
She asks about employer funding before spending her own money.
She frames the downside as wasted evenings, not wasted career.

steps.text: Enrol in one evening module in software quality
Save £100 a month towards a six-week cushion
Use AI tools daily at work and note where they fail

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means my generation gets a real chance. At work I'd say let's plan the intake of graduates now. To friends I'd say you've got time to pick something you like. Online I'd say governments should start building the retraining system today, not in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I feel hopeful, and a bit guilty about it. Ten years is long enough to pay off most of my loan, get a proper qualification and maybe a house deposit. I'd like to move into safety testing, where laws mean a human has to sign things off. The risk is that I get comfortable and don't change when I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish a part-time master's in software engineering, maybe in six years, with the firm paying some of it. I'd save steadily, aiming for six months of expenses by 2030. I'd also switch to a role that blends testing and AI oversight early. And I'd help my parents get their bakery online, which they've asked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like there's room to breathe. I still carry the money worry, but the world won't end in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're afraid of getting comfortable. How would you catch that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set one date every year, my birthday, to look at job ads and see what's asked for that I can't do. If the list has grown, I act. It's a boring trick, but I know I won't change unless something forces me, so I'd build the force myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope your parents' bakery looks like by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still open, honestly. They'd have an online ordering page and a van delivering to offices. I'd build the page myself in a weekend. If thinking-AI makes my job shaky, the bakery at least sells something people physically eat, and I find that comforting.

say: I'd say governments should build the **retraining** system today, not in year nine.
I'd tell friends they have **time** to pick something they like.
think: I feel **hopeful** and a bit guilty, because ten years lets me clear much of my loan.
The risk is getting **comfortable** and not changing when I should.
do: Finish a part-time **master's** in software engineering, with the firm paying some.
Build my parents' **bakery** an online ordering page.
feel: Room to **breathe**, though the money worry stays.
S4.quote: I know I won't change unless something forces me, so I'd build the force myself.
fieldNote: The **long runway** moves her to calm; money worry remains but is no longer urgent.
She builds an annual checkpoint against her own tendency to wait for proof.
Family ties give her a practical project.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in software engineering in two years
Save six months of expenses by 2030
Build my parents' bakery an online ordering page in a weekend

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Two years isn't enough to retrain, and my parents can't catch me. What would help is wages while you retrain, a firm that tells juniors honestly where they stand, and some protection on student loan repayments if you lose your job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think graduates my age are being dramatic. We're not. We borrowed to get into the one field everyone said was safe. I'd like someone to say clearly what the plan is for us, even if the plan is small.

headlineQuote: We borrowed to get into the one field everyone said was safe.
portrait: Tara is a 22-year-old computer science graduate working as a **junior tester** at a Coventry logistics software firm on a graduate contract.
She is progressive and steady: she uses AI now and then and moves once something is proven.
Her parents run a small bakery and cannot help, so the **loan** is hers alone.
She is anxious when little changes because a lost client already scared her, and alarmed at two years.
Her plans are modest and specific: automated tests, a part-time module, and a cheaper flat.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture worries her most, with no time to retrain and no family safety net.
whatWouldHelp: Wages while retraining, honest talk from her firm, and **protection** on loan repayments if she loses work.
